title: Promises and async/await, error handling
summary: async/await is syntax over Promises: await suspends the function without blocking the thread, and try/catch around await catches the rejection.

examples.title: Sequential awaits, try/catch, and what NOT to do

annotations.note: A fake fetch returning a Promise: the async story starts here. A rejected Promise is the async equivalent of a thrown exception.

await suspends this function, not the page: the event loop keeps running other work. A Go channel receive likewise blocks only its own goroutine; the difference is that in JS every caller up the chain has to be async to wait for the result.

try/catch catches the rejection. Without it the rejection travels up to the caller, and if nobody handles it the run fails with an unhandled rejection. Unlike Go's error results, nothing in the types tells you it can happen.
The naive version: starting both awaits but catching nothing here. Promise.all (next lesson) is the tool when you truly want parallel.

use_cases: Any fetch/XHR call, IndexedDB, timers — every browser async API returns Promises
Sequential async steps where step 2 needs step 1's result
strengths: Async code reads top-to-bottom like sync code, unlike callback nesting
try/catch catches async and sync errors alike inside an async function
Composable: Promises are values — pass them, race them, allSettled them
weaknesses: await in a loop serializes independent work — the classic accidental waterfall
Errors outside try/catch become unhandled rejections; nothing forces you to catch
Forgetting await silently yields a Promise where you expected a value

pitfalls.title: await inside a for loop over independent items
pitfalls.detail: Each await waits for the previous one: N requests take N times longer. Use Promise.all.

pitfalls.title: Mixing callbacks and Promises
pitfalls.detail: An async function's returned Promise is ignored by callback APIs. Pick one style per call chain.

pitfalls.title: try/catch that swallows the error shape
pitfalls.detail: catch (e) gives unknown in strict TS; narrow before reading e.message.

quiz.q: What does await do to the rest of the page?
quiz.why: await parks the function and returns control to the event loop; other work continues.

quiz.q: How do you catch a rejected Promise from an awaited call?
quiz.why: await rethrows the rejection as an exception inside the async function, so try/catch works.

body:
## Concept

A Promise is a value that isn't ready yet: pending, then fulfilled or rejected. `await p`
suspends the enclosing async function until `p` settles; a rejection becomes a throw you can
catch with try/catch. `async function` always returns a Promise, even of `undefined`.

## Coming from C/C++/Java/Python/JS

- Python: `async/await` keywords are nearly identical; JS Promises ≈ Futures, but eager
  (already running when created), unlike Python coroutines that need a loop to drive them.
- Java: `CompletableFuture.thenApply` chains; async/await is the linear spelling of those.
- Go: no equivalent — you'd start a goroutine and use a channel for the result. The event
  loop has one thread, so "suspend this function" replaces "block this goroutine".

## Design notes

The naive version in the example shows the shape the next lesson fixes with combinators.
Rule of thumb: sequential awaits when there's a data dependency; `Promise.all` when there
isn't; `Promise.allSettled` when partial failure is acceptable. Async/await is the interface
to the event loop — the concurrency lesson compares this with goroutines directly.

expected.fetch-sequence:
first done; second done
a done; b done
